prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: The GLP-1 discovery chain is unusually complete: the incretin effect and the secretion and action of the native peptide (Holst), proglucagon processing and the biology of GLP-1 and GLP-2 (Drucker), and identification and synthesis of the active truncated GLP-1(7-36) form (Mojsov). Together these explain why the hormone could be turned into a drug. The result is a new therapeutic class for type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal benefit shown in large randomized trials. The change in the field is discernible and the findings have been confirmed independently over three decades. Five of six opening ballots placed it first, and I accept that colleagues weigh its maturity and consequence more heavily than I did when I ranked it third. My own first choice, the unfolded protein response (B007), remains a conceptually clean discovery, but its medical payoff is still mainly in basic biology and preclinical work, and the broad agreement around B045 deserves to be taken seriously on the merits rather than discounted.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weak point. The priority history of the active peptide among Mojsov, Habener and Holst is contested, and Habener is not on the credited list, so a prize built around the peptide-identification step could be unfair to someone the ballot does not let us name. Excluding Knudsen means the prize honours physiology and peptide biology and not the pharmacology that produced liraglutide and semaglutide, which is where most of the patient benefit actually comes from. A prize that credits only the academic discoverers risks being read as incomplete, while one that credits an industrial scientist risks blurring discovery with development. The three-person cap forces one of those choices.

responses.point: Holst, Drucker and Mojsov form a defensible physiology trio, with Knudsen's long-acting analogue work treated as industrial development and left out.
responses.response: I agree with the principle that the prize should rest on the discovery of the hormone's biology. Where I qualify it is that Mojsov's place depends on a priority claim that is contested with Habener, and neither of us can settle that from the supplied credit. I would keep her on the proposal because the identification of the active form is a necessary link in the chain, but I would not describe the trio as clean, and I would want the committee to record that uncertainty openly.

responses.point: Holst, Drucker and Knudsen form a coherent trio that runs from physiology through to translation, and Mojsov's role is left as an open credit question.
responses.response: I take the argument for Knudsen seriously, because the translation into long-acting analogues is the step that reached patients. My reservation is that the prize has historically distinguished the discovery of a mechanism from its industrial development, and the drug design does not by itself show a new biological principle. I would give weight to the active peptide as the discovery that made the drug design possible. I regard this as a real disagreement and I do not think it resolves cleanly in either direction, so I hold Knudsen as the main alternative name and not as a settled exclusion.

responses.point: The unfolded protein response is a clean, mature, conceptually original two-person discovery (Walter and Mori), ranked second after GLP-1, with other arms of the response outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with your assessment of the science and it was my own first choice. I would qualify one point. You note that PERK, ATF6 and the work of Ron and Kaufman fall outside the credited list, and I think that is a larger problem than the ballot makes it look, because a prize for the response as a whole would be open to the charge of leaving out parts of it. That is why I now put it as an alternative to B045, not as the preferred prize, even though I still think it is the strongest purely basic-science candidate.

responses.point: Antisense correction of SMN2 splicing (B035) and BCR-ABL inhibition (B018) are exceptional mechanism-to-therapy stories, with Krainer and Bennett fitting a compact two-person prize.
responses.response: I agree that nusinersen is a compelling mechanism-to-therapy story, but I do not think the credited names carry it to a prize at this point. As you note yourself, the discovery of the SMN1 gene and the broader antisense platform are not captured, and I would be uneasy rewarding one drug before the committee has decided how to treat RNA therapeutics as a whole. I therefore do not include it among my alternatives, though I accept it could look different in a later round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will credit the contested priority for the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov versus Habener, who is not on the supplied list) and how much weight that step should carry.
Whether the prize should recognise the physiology of the hormone or also the drug-development step (Knudsen), given the three-laureate cap.
Whether the omission of other arms of the unfolded protein response (PERK, ATF6) weakens B007 as a fallback.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records past nuclear-receptor co-authorship with Ronald Evans and collaboration with Johan Ericson, and about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson and one with Abdel El Manira. None of these people are credited on any shortlisted ballot, so no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the candidates I discuss.
